newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE weighs decision on Bosnia's local polls.
newsitem.headline: OSCE weighs decision on Bosnia's local polls.

text.p: International officials organising Bosnia's local polls are faced with a stark choice -- to press ahead with imperfect elections or postpone them and risk unsupervised voting in the future, diplomats say.

"The OSCE has to decide between fiasco, disaster-prone local elections in November or try to get written assurances for the extension of the mandate and postpone them for next year," a Western official told Reuters.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) supervised Bosnia's first post-war general elections on September 14 but had to postpone local polls in August because of irregularities in voter registration.
Now the OSCE is facing a boycott from Serb leaders who say they will not take part in internationally-organised municipal elections in November.
"If the OSCE does not win the agreement on its mandate extension, then it can only push ahead with such elections or cancel them altogether," said the official, who asked not to be named.
He said unsupervised elections in Bosnia would give nationalist leaders a free hand to create their own rules, which would only serve their interests and fail to reunite the war-torn country.
The municipal elections, set for November 23 and 24, are viewed as the last chance for Bosnia to be reunited after a war that divided the country into ethnic ghettoes.
Voting for local officials could pave the way for refugees to return to communities they had been expelled from during 43-months of war.
But critics say polls held in a country with no freedom of movement, uncooperative nationalist leaders and unresolved disputes about voting by displaced people cannot be a success.
"The best solution would be if everybody agreed to an extension of the mandate and then OSCE could postpone elections with a mind at peace," said one diplomat.

U.S. President Bill Clinton's envoy to the Balkans, John Kornblum, flew to Sarajevo on Monday and was expected to apply pressure on the country's national leaders to agree to OSCE-supervised local elections sometime in the future.
He is also due to hold talks with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic in Banja Luka on Tuesday and anaysts believe the negotiations could produce some kind of a compromise.
Western mediators hope the threat of withholding reconstruction aid could push all three nationalist parties, particularly the Serbs, to reach an agreement.
The OSCE's head of mission in Bosnia, Robert Frowick, has been engaged in intense negotiations with the Serbs over the past several weeks.
Plavsic earlier this month offered the OSCE a monitoring role in local elections to be organised by a Serb republic government elected in the September poll.

Last week, she raised the stakes in her standoff with the international community when she declared that she had said 'no' to Frowick, citing security problems in villages in Serb territory resettled by Moslem refugees.
Frowick has also come under mounting pressure within the international community to postpone the polls.
Diplomats from countries involved in the Bosnian peace process have warned that the OSCE needs more time to ensure higher standards for the politically-sensitive vote.
